text: Let the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=4$ intersect x-axis at the points A$(a,0)$, $a>0$ and B$(b,0)$. Let $P(2\cos α,2\sin α)$, $0<α<\frac{π}{2}$ and $Q(2\cos β,2\sin β)$ be two points such that $(α-β)=\frac{π}{2}$. Then the point of intersection of AQ and BP lies on :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 28th January Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
[IMG]

The circle is $x^{2}+y^{2}=2^{2}$ (radius $r=2$ ).

Intersection with $𝐱$-axis: Setting $y=0$ gives $x^{2}=4\Rightarrow x=\pm 2$.

Since $a>0,A=(2,0)$.

Therefore, $B=(-2,0)$.

Points $P$ and $Q$ :

$P=(2\cos α,2\sin α)$

$Q=(2\cos β,2\sin β)$

Let point of intersection of $AQ$ .& $BP$ be $R(h,k)$.

So, we need to find locus of points of intersection of $AQ&BP$.

Slope of $BP=$ slope of $BR$

$\begin{array}{l} \dfrac{k-0}{h-(-2)}=\dfrac{2\sin α-0}{2\cos α+2} \\ \dfrac{k}{h+2}=\dfrac{\sin α}{\cos α+1}\Rightarrow \dfrac{k}{h+2}=\dfrac{2\sin \frac{α}{2}\cos \frac{α}{2}}{2\cos ^{2}\frac{α}{2}} \\ \dfrac{k}{h+2}=\tan \dfrac{α}{2}...(i) \end{array}$

Similarly, slope of $QA=$ slope of $QR$

$\begin{array}{l} \dfrac{2\sin β-0}{2\cos β-2}=\dfrac{k-0}{h-2} \\ \dfrac{\sin β}{\cos β-1}=\dfrac{k}{h-2}\Rightarrow \dfrac{2\sin \frac{β}{2}\cos \frac{β}{2}}{-2\sin ^{2}\frac{β}{2}}=\dfrac{k}{h-2} \\ -\cot \dfrac{β}{2}=\dfrac{k}{h-2} \\ \cot \dfrac{β}{2}=\dfrac{k}{2-h}\Rightarrow \tan \dfrac{β}{2}=\dfrac{2-h}{k} \end{array}$

Given,

$\begin{array}{l} α-β=\dfrac{π}{2}\Rightarrow \dfrac{α}{2}-\dfrac{β}{2}=\dfrac{π}{4} \\ \tan \left (\dfrac{α}{2}-\dfrac{β}{2}\right )=\tan \dfrac{π}{4} \\ \dfrac{\tan \frac{α}{2}-\tan \frac{β}{2}}{1+\tan \frac{α}{2}\tan \frac{β}{2}}=1 \end{array}$

Substitute

$\tan \frac{α}{2}=\frac{k}{h+2},\tan \frac{β}{2}=\frac{2-h}{k}$

$\begin{array}{l} \dfrac{\frac{k}{h+2}-\frac{2-h}{k}}{1+\left (\frac{k}{h+2}\right )\left (\frac{2-h}{k}\right )}=1 \\ \dfrac{k}{h+2}+\dfrac{h-2}{k}=1+\left (\dfrac{k}{h+2}\right )\left (\dfrac{2-h}{k}\right ) \\ \dfrac{k^{2}+h^{2}-4}{(h+2)k}=\dfrac{4k}{(h+2)k} \\ \dfrac{k^{2}+h^{2}-4}{(h+2)k}=\dfrac{4k}{(h+2)k} \\ k^{2}+h^{2}-4=4k \\ k^{2}+h^{2}-4k-4=0 \end{array}$

Replace $(h,k)\to (x,y)$

$x^{2}+y^{2}-4y-4=0$

Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $x\frac{dy}{dx}-y=x^{2}\cot x$, $x\in (0,π)$. If $y\left (\frac{π}{2}\right )=\frac{π}{2}$, then
$6y\left (\frac{π}{6}\right )-8y\left (\frac{π}{4}\right )$ is equal to :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 28th January Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The given equation is:

$x\frac{dy}{dx}-y=x^{2}\cot x$

To get it into the standard form $\frac{dy}{dx}+P(x)y=Q(x)$, we divide the entire equation by $x$ :

$\frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{1}{x}y=x\cot x$

Here, $P(x)=-\frac{1}{x}$ and $Q(x)=x\cot x$.

Finding the Integrating Factor (I.F.)

The integrating factor is calculated as:

$\text{I.F.}=e^{\int P(x)dx}=e^{\int -\frac{1}{x}dx}=e^{-\ln x}=e^{\ln \left (x^{-1}\right )}=\frac{1}{x}$

The solution to the differential equation is:

$\begin{array}{l} y\cdot (I.F.)=\int Q(x)\cdot (I.F.)dx \\ \dfrac{y}{x}=\int (x\cot x)\cdot \dfrac{1}{x}dx \\ \dfrac{y}{x}=\int \cot xdx \\ \dfrac{y}{x}=\ln (\sin x)+C \\ y=x\ln (\sin x)+Cx \end{array}$

Applying the Initial Condition

We are given $y\left (\frac{π}{2}\right )=\frac{π}{2}$. Plugging these values in:

$\frac{π}{2}=\frac{π}{2}\ln \left (\sin \frac{π}{2}\right )+C\left (\frac{π}{2}\right )$

So, the particular solution is $y=x\ln (\sin x)+x$.

We need to find the value of $6y\left (\frac{π}{6}\right )-8y\left (\frac{π}{4}\right )$.

Calculate $y\left (\frac{π}{6}\right )$ :

$y\left (\frac{π}{6}\right )=\frac{π}{6}\ln \left (\sin \frac{π}{6}\right )+\frac{π}{6}=\frac{π}{6}\ln \left (\frac{1}{2}\right )+\frac{π}{6}=\frac{π}{6}(1-\ln 2)$

Calculate $y\left (\frac{π}{4}\right )$ :

$y\left (\frac{π}{4}\right )=\frac{π}{4}\ln \left (\sin \frac{π}{4}\right )+\frac{π}{4}=\frac{π}{4}\ln \left (\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right )+\frac{π}{4}=\frac{π}{4}\ln \left (2^{-1/2}\right )+\frac{π}{4}=\frac{π}{4}\left (1-\frac{1}{2}\ln 2\right )$

Calculate $y\left (\frac{π}{4}\right )$ :

$y\left (\frac{π}{4}\right )=\frac{π}{4}\ln \left (\sin \frac{π}{4}\right )+\frac{π}{4}=\frac{π}{4}\ln \left (\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right )+\frac{π}{4}=\frac{π}{4}\ln \left (2^{-1/2}\right )+\frac{π}{4}=\frac{π}{4}\left (1-\frac{1}{2}\ln 2\right )$

Now, substitute these into the expression:

$\begin{array}{ll} 6y\left (\dfrac{π}{6}\right )-8y\left (\dfrac{π}{4}\right ) & =6\left [\dfrac{π}{6}(1-\ln 2)\right ]-8\left [\dfrac{π}{4}\left (1-\dfrac{1}{2}\ln 2\right )\right ]=π(1-\ln 2)-2π\left (1-\dfrac{1}{2}\ln 2\right ) \\ = & π-π\ln 2-2π+π\ln 2=-π \end{array}$

sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 28th January Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Point $P(3,2,1)$ 

Let Line $L_{1}:\frac{x-1}{1}=\frac{y}{2}=\frac{z-1}{1}$ and $L_{2}:\frac{x-9}{3}=\frac{y-9}{2}=\frac{z-5}{-2}$

Direction vector of $L_{1}:(1,2,1)$

Let the first line be $L_{1}:\frac{x-1}{1}=\frac{y}{2}=\frac{z-1}{1}=λ$. 

Any general point $M$ on this line is $M(λ+1,2λ,λ+1)$.

If $M$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $P(3,2,1)$ to $L_{1}$, the direction ratio of $PM$ is $(λ-2,2λ-2,λ)$. 

Since $PM⟂L_{1}$ : Since $PM⟂L_{1}$ :

$1(λ-2)+2(2λ-2)+1(λ)=0$

$\Rightarrow$ $λ-2+4λ-4+λ=0⟹6λ=6⟹λ=1$

The foot of the perpendicular $M$ is $(2,2,2)$. Since $M$ is the midpoint of $PQ$, where $Q$ is $(a,b,c)$ :

$\frac{a+3}{2}=2⟹a=1$

$\frac{b+2}{2}=2⟹b=2$

$\frac{c+1}{2}=2⟹c=3$

So, $Q=(1,2,3)$.

Find the distance of $Q(1,2,3)$ from the second line

The second line is $L_{2}:\frac{x-9}{3}=\frac{y-9}{2}=\frac{z-5}{-2}=μ$. 

Let $A(9,9,5)$ be a point on $L_{2}$ and $d=3\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$ be its direction vector.

The vector $AQ=(1-9)\hat{i}+(2-9)\hat{j}+(3-5)\hat{k}=-8\hat{i}-7\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$.

The distance $D$ of a point from a line is given by:

Distance of point from line :

$D=\frac{|AQ\leftarrow \times ⃗{d}|}{|⃗{d}|}$

Cross product

$\begin{array}{lllllll} AQ\leftarrow \times ⃗{d}=\left |\begin{array}{lll} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ -8 & -7 & -2 \\ 3 & 2 & -2 \end{array}\right | \\ =\hat{i}[(-7)(-2)-(-2)(2)]-\hat{j}[(-8)(-2)-(-2)(3)]+\hat{k}[(-8)(2)-(-7)(3)] \\ =\hat{i}(14+4)-\hat{j}(16+6)+\hat{k}(-16+21) \\ AQ\leftarrow \times ⃗{d}=18\hat{i}-22\hat{j}+5\hat{k} \end{array}$

Magnitudes

$\begin{array}{l} |AQ\leftarrow \times ⃗{d}|=\sqrt{18^{2}+(-22)^{2}+5^{2}}=\sqrt{833} \\ |⃗{d}|=\sqrt{3^{2}+2^{2}+(-2)^{2}}=\sqrt{17} \end{array}$

Distance of point from line

$D=\frac{|AQ\leftarrow \times ⃗{d}|}{|⃗{d}|}=\sqrt{\frac{833}{17}}=\sqrt{49}=7$

Considering the principal values of inverse trigonometric functions, the value of the expression
$\tan \left (2\sin ^{-1}\left (\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\right )-2\cos ^{-1}\left (\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\right )\right )$is equal to :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 28th January Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Simplify the individual components

Let $α=\sin ^{-1}\left (\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\right )$ and $β=\cos ^{-1}\left (\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\right )$.

For $α$ : Since $\sin α=\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}$, using Pythagoras' theorem (base $=\sqrt{(\sqrt{13})^{2}-2^{2}}=3$ ), we get:

$\tan α=\frac{2}{3}$

For $β$ : Since $\cos β=\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}$, using Pythagoras' theorem (perpendicular $=\sqrt{(\sqrt{10})^{2}-3^{2}}=1$ ), we get:

$\tan β=\frac{1}{3}$

Rewrite the expression

The expression becomes: $\tan (2α-2β)=\tan [2(α-β)]$.

First, find $\tan (α-β)$ using the formula $\tan (A-B)=\frac{\tan A-\tan B}{1+\tan A\tan B}$

$\tan (α-β)=\frac{\frac{2}{3}-\frac{1}{3}}{1+\left (\frac{2}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\right )}=\frac{\frac{1}{3}}{1+\frac{2}{9}}=\frac{\frac{1}{3}}{\frac{11}{9}}=\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{9}{11}=\frac{3}{11}$

Calculate the final value

Now, use the double angle formula $\tan (2θ)=\frac{2\tan θ}{1-\tan ^{2}θ}$, where $θ=(α-β)$ :

$\begin{array}{l} \tan [2(α-β)]=\dfrac{2\left (\frac{3}{11}\right )}{1-\left (\frac{3}{11}\right )^{2}} \\ \tan [2(α-β)]=\dfrac{\frac{6}{11}}{1-\frac{9}{121}}=\dfrac{\frac{6}{11}}{\frac{112}{121}} \\ \tan [2(α-β)]=\dfrac{6}{11}\cdot \dfrac{121}{112}=\dfrac{6\cdot 11}{112}=\dfrac{66}{112}=\dfrac{33}{56} \end{array}$

text: Let the arithmetic mean of $\frac{1}{a}$ and $\frac{1}{b}$ be $\frac{5}{16}$, $a>2$. If $α$ is such that $a$, $4$, $α$, $b$ are in A.P., then the equation $αx^{2}-ax+2(α-2b)=0$ has :
options: one root in $(1,4)$ and another in $(-2,0)$
one root in $(0,2)$ and another in $(-4,-2)$
complex roots of magnitude less than $2$
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 28th January Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The arithmetic mean of $\frac{1}{a}$ and $\frac{1}{b}$ is $\frac{5}{16}$.

$\frac{\frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{b}}{2}=\frac{5}{16}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{b}=\frac{5}{8}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{a+b}{ab}=\frac{5}{8}$

$\Rightarrow 8(a+b)=5ab...(i)$

$a,4,α,b$ are in A.P. Let the common difference be $d$.

(A). $4=a+d⟹d=4-a$

(B). $α=a+2d=a+2(4-a)=8-a$

(C). $b=a+3d=a+3(4-a)=12-2a$

Solve for $a,b$, and $α$

Substitute $b=12-2a$ into equation (1) :

$\begin{array}{l} 8(a+12-2a)=5a(12-2a) \\ 8(12-a)=60a-10a^{2} \\ 96-8a=60a-10a^{2} \\ 10a^{2}-68a+96=0 \\ 5a^{2}-34a+48=0 \end{array}$

Using the quadratic formula: $a=\frac{34\pm \sqrt{34^{2}-4(5)(48)}}{2(5)}=\frac{34\pm \sqrt{1156-960}}{10}=\frac{34\pm 14}{10}$

$a=\frac{48}{10}=4.8,a=\frac{20}{10}=2\text{(Discarded because the problem states}a>2\text{)}$

With $a=4.8:α=8-4.8=𝟑\mathbf{.}𝟐,b=12-2(4.8)=12-9.6=𝟐\mathbf{.}𝟒$

Analyze the Quadratic Equation

The given equation is $αx^{2}-ax+2(α-2b)=0$. Substitute the values:

$\begin{array}{l} 3.2x^{2}-4.8x+2(3.2-2(2.4))=0 \\ 3.2x^{2}-4.8x+2(3.2-4.8)=0 \\ 3.2x^{2}-4.8x-3.2=0 \\ 2x^{2}-3x-2=0 \end{array}$

Factorise $(2x+1)(x-2)=0$

The roots are $x=2$ and $x=-0.5$.

Looking at the options: Root $x=2$ lies in the interval $(1,4)$. Root $x=-0.5$ lies in the interval $(-2,0)$.

Given below are two statements :

Statement I : The function $f:\mathrm{ℝ}\to \mathrm{ℝ}$ defined by $f(x)=\frac{x}{1+|x|}$ is one-one.

Statement II : The function $f:\mathrm{ℝ}\to \mathrm{ℝ}$ defined by $f(x)=\frac{x^{2}+4x-30}{x^{2}-8x+18}$ is many-one.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below :
options: Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 28th January Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Statement I: for $x\geq 0$, $f(x)=\dfrac{x}{1+x}$ with $f^{'}(x)=\dfrac{1}{(1+x)^{2}}>0$; for $x<0$, $f(x)=\dfrac{x}{1-x}$ with $f^{'}(x)=\dfrac{1}{(1-x)^{2}}>0$.

$f$ is continuous at $0$, so it is strictly increasing on $\mathrm{ℝ}$ and hence one-one. Statement I is true.

Statement II: the denominator $x^{2}-8x+18=(x-4)^{2}+2>0$ for every real $x$, so $f$ is defined on $\mathrm{ℝ}$.

The numerator $x^{2}+4x-30=0$ has two real roots $x=-2\pm \sqrt{34}$, so $f(-2+\sqrt{34})=f(-2-\sqrt{34})=0$.

Two different inputs have the same image, so $f$ is many-one. Statement II is true.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

text: Let P be a point in the plane of the vectors $AB\leftarrow =3\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ and $AC\leftarrow =\hat{i}-\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ such that P is equidistant from the lines AB and AC. If $|AP\leftarrow |=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}$, then the area of the triangle ABP is :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 28th January Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Point $P$ is equidistant from the lines $AB$ and $AC$. Geometrically, this means point $P$ must lie on the angle bisector of the angle formed by vectors $AB$ and $AC$.

First, we find the unit vectors along $AB$ and $AC$ :

$|AB|=\sqrt{3^{2}+1^{2}+(-1)^{2}}=\sqrt{11}$

$|AC|=\sqrt{1^{2}+(-1)^{2}+3^{2}}=\sqrt{11}$

Since the magnitudes are equal, the angle bisector $v$ is simply the sum of the two vectors:

$\begin{array}{l} v=AB+AC=(3+1)\hat{i}+(1-1)\hat{j}+(-1+3)\hat{k}=4\hat{i}+2\hat{k} \end{array}$

The vector $AP$ will be in the direction of the unit vector $\hat{v}$ :

$\hat{v}=\frac{4\hat{i}+2\hat{k}}{\sqrt{4^{2}+2^{2}}}=\frac{4\hat{i}+2\hat{k}}{\sqrt{20}}=\frac{4\hat{i}+2\hat{k}}{2\sqrt{5}}=\frac{2\hat{i}+\hat{k}}{\sqrt{5}}$

Determine Vector $AP$

Given that $|AP|=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}$, we can write:

$AP=|AP|\hat{v}=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}\left (\frac{2\hat{i}+\hat{k}}{\sqrt{5}}\right )=\frac{1}{2}(2\hat{i}+\hat{k})=\hat{i}+\frac{1}{2}\hat{k}$

Calculate the Area of Triangle $ABP$

The area of a triangle formed by two vectors $AB$ and $AP$ is given by the formula:

$\text{Area}=\frac{1}{2}|AB\leftarrow \times AP\leftarrow |$

First, compute the cross product $AB\times AP$ :

$\begin{array}{lllllll} AB\leftarrow \times AP\leftarrow =\left |\begin{array}{lll} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 3 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & \frac{1}{2} \end{array}\right | \\ =\hat{i}\left (\dfrac{1}{2}-0\right )-\hat{j}\left (\dfrac{3}{2}-(-1)\right )+\hat{k}(0-1) \\ =\dfrac{1}{2}\hat{i}-\dfrac{5}{2}\hat{j}-\hat{k} \\ |AB\leftarrow \times AP\leftarrow |=\sqrt{\left (\dfrac{1}{2}\right )^{2}+\left (-\dfrac{5}{2}\right )^{2}+(-1)^{2}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{25}{4}+1}=\sqrt{\dfrac{26}{4}+\dfrac{4}{4}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{30}{4}}=\dfrac{\sqrt{30}}{2} \end{array}$

Finally, the area of the triangle is:

Area $=\frac{1}{2}\left (\frac{\sqrt{30}}{2}\right )=\frac{\sqrt{30}}{4}$

text: Let $f(x)=\int \frac{dx}{x^{2/3}+2x^{1/2}},$ be such that $f(0)=-26+24\log _{e}(2)$. If $f(1)=a+b\log _{e}(3)$, where $a,b\in \mathrm{ℤ}$, then $a+b$ is equal to :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 28th January Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Given

$f(x)=\int \frac{dx}{x^{2/3}+2x^{1/2}},$

$f(0)=-26+24\ln 2\text{and}$

$f(1)=a+b\ln 3,a,b\in \mathrm{ℤ}$

Use substitution Let $x=t^{6}⟹dx=6t^{5}dt$

$\begin{array}{l} x^{2/3}=\left (t^{6}\right )^{2/3}=t^{4} \\ x^{1/2}=\left (t^{6}\right )^{1/2}=t^{3} \end{array}$

Substituting these into the integral :

$f(x)=\int \frac{6t^{5}}{t^{4}+2t^{3}}dt=\int \frac{6t^{5}}{t^{3}(t+2)}dt=\int \frac{6t^{2}}{t+2}dt$

manipulate

$\frac{t^{2}}{t+2}=\frac{\left (t^{2}-4\right )+4}{t+2}=\frac{(t-2)(t+2)+4}{t+2}=(t-2)+\frac{4}{t+2}$

Now, integrate term by term:

$\begin{array}{l} f(x)=6\int \left (t-2+\dfrac{4}{t+2}\right )dt \\ f(x)=6\left [\dfrac{t^{2}}{2}-2t+4\ln |t+2|\right ]+C \end{array}$

$f(x)=3t^{2}-12t+24\ln |t+2|+C$

Back-substitute $t=x^{1/6}$ :

$f(x)=3x^{1/3}-12x^{1/6}+24\ln \left |x^{1/6}+2\right |+C$

Finding the Constant $C$

We are given the initial condition $f(0)=-26+24\ln (2)$ :

$\begin{array}{l} f(0)=3(0)-12(0)+24\ln (0+2)+C \\ -26+24\ln (2)=24\ln (2)+C⟹𝐂=-𝟐 𝟔 \end{array}$

So, the complete function is:

$f(x)=3x^{1/3}-12x^{1/6}+24\ln \left (x^{1/6}+2\right )-26$

Solving for $a$ and $b$

Now we evaluate $f(1)$ :

$\begin{array}{l} f(1)=3(1)^{1/3}-12(1)^{1/6}+24\ln \left (1^{1/6}+2\right )-26 \\ f(1)=3-12+24\ln (3)-26 \\ f(1)=-35+24\ln (3) \end{array}$

Comparing this to the given form $f(1)=a+b\ln (3)$ :

$a=-35\text{and}b=24$

Then

$a+b=-35+24=-𝟏 𝟏$

text: An ellipse has its center at $(1,-2)$, one focus at $(3,-2)$ and one vertex at $(5,-2)$. Then the length of its latus rectum is :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 28th January Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Given

Center of ellipse : $(1,-2)$

Focus : $(3,-2)$

Vertex : $(5,-2)$


[IMG]

The center, focus, and vertex all have the same $y$-coordinate $(-2)$, which means the major axis of the ellipse is horizontal (parallel to the $x$-axis).

Find $a$ (semi-major axis)

Distance from center to vertex :

$a=|5-1|=4$

Find $c$ (distance from center to focus)

$c=|3-1|=2$

Find $b$ using ellipse relation

$c^{2}=a^{2}-b^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $2^{2}=4^{2}-b^{2}$

$\Rightarrow 4=16-b^{2}$

$\Rightarrow b^{2}=12$

$\Rightarrow b=2\sqrt{3}$

Length of latus rectum

For an ellipse :

Length of latus rectum $=\frac{2b^{2}}{a}$

$=\frac{2(12)}{4}=6$

text:
Given below are two statements :
Statement I :
$25^{13}+20^{13}+8^{13}+3^{13}$ is divisible by 7.
Statement II :
The integral part of $(7+4\sqrt{3})^{25}$ is an odd number.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below :
options: Statement I is false but Statement II is true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 28th January Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Statement I : $25^{13}+20^{13}+8^{13}+3^{13}$ is divisible by 7.

Key concept : If $n$ is odd, $x^{n}+y^{n}=(x+y)\left (x^{n-1}-x^{n-2}y+x^{n-3}y^{2}-\cdots -xy^{n-2}+y^{n-1} \right.$ ) So, $x^{n}+y^{n}$ is divisible by $x+y$.

In the given statement :

$25^{13}+3^{13}$ is divisible by $25+3=28$.

$25^{13}+3^{13}$ is also divisible by 7 because 28 is divisible by 7 .

So, $25^{13}+3^{13}=7\cdot I_{1}$.........(1) ( $I_{1}$ is a positive integer).

Similarly :

$20^{13}+8^{13}$ is divisible by $20+8=28$.

$20^{13}+8^{13}$ is divisible by 7.

So, $20^{13}+8^{13}=7\cdot I_{2}$ ..........(2) ( $I_{2}$ is a positive integer).

Add (1) & (2) :

$25^{13}+3^{13}+20^{13}+8^{13}=7(I_{1}+I_{2})$

So, $25^{13}+20^{13}+8^{13}+3^{13}$ is divisible by 7 . Statement I is true.

Statement II : The integral part of $(7+4\sqrt{3})^{25}$ is an odd number.

Let $X=(7+4\sqrt{3})^{25}$. Let $I$ be the integral part and $f$ be the fractional part ( $0<f<1$ ), so $X=I+f$. Now, consider $f^{'}=(7-4\sqrt{3})^{25}$. Since $4\sqrt{3}=\sqrt{48}$, and $\sqrt{49}=7$, we know $0<7-4\sqrt{3}<1$. Therefore, $0<f^{'}<1$.

Adding the two expansions:

$(7+4\sqrt{3})^{25}+(7-4\sqrt{3})^{25}=I+f+f^{'}$

Using the binomial expansion $(a+b)^{n}+(a-b)^{n}=2\left [a^{n}+\left (n2\right )a^{n-2}b^{2}+\ldots \right ]$, we see that the sum is always an even integer because of the factor of 2 .

$I+f+f^{'}=\text{Even Integer}$

Since $I$ is an integer, $f+f^{'}$ must also be an integer. Given $0<f<1$ and $0<f^{'}<1$, the only possible integer value for their sum is $f+f^{'}=1$.

$I+1=\text{Even Integer}$

$I=\text{Even Integer}-1=\text{Odd Integer}$

The integral part I is indeed an odd number. Statement II is True.

solution.body:

Analyze Set $A$ :

The set $A$ is defined as $\{z\in \mathrm{ℂ}:|z-2|\leq 4\}$.

This represents a circle (and its interior) centered at $(2,0)$ with a radius $r=4$.

The circle extends from $x=-2$ to $x=6$ along the real axis.

Analyze Set $B$ :

The set $B$ is defined as $\{z\in \mathrm{ℂ}:|z-2|+|z+2|=5\}$.

By the definition of an ellipse, the sum of distances from two fixed points (foci) is constant.

Here, the foci are $F_{1}(2,0)$ and $F_{2}(-2,0)$, and the length of the major axis $2a=5$, so $a=2.5$.

The distance between foci is $2ae=4$, so $e=\frac{4}{5}=0.8$.

To find $\max \{|z_{1}-z_{2}|:z_{1}\in A$ and $z_{2}\in B\}$ This means maximize the distance between a point $z_{1}$ in the circle and a point $z_{2}$ on the ellipse.

The furthest point in set $A$ (the circle) is at the rightmost edge, $z_{1}=(2+4,0)=(6,0)$.

The furthest point in set $B$ (the ellipse) from $z_{1}$ is at its leftmost edge, $z_{2}=(-2.5,0)$.

Maximum Distance $|z_{1}-z_{2}|=|6-(-2.5)|=|6+2.5|=8.5=\frac{17}{2}$

solution.body:

Focus $A$ : The focus is $(a,0)$, which is $(2,0)$.

Define Parametric Points for $B$ and $C$ : Let the two distinct points of intersection be $B$ a $C$. Using parametric coordinates $\left (at^{2},2at\right )$ :

Point $B=\left (2t_{1}^{2},4t_{1}\right )$

Use the Centroid Formula : The centroid $G(x,y)$ of a triangle with vertices $(x_{1},y_{1}),(x_{2},y_{2})$, and $(x_{3},y_{3})$ is:

$G=\left (\frac{x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{3}}{3},\frac{y_{1}+y_{2}+y_{3}}{3}\right )$

Use the Centroid Property : The centroid of triangle $ABC$ with vertices $A(2,0)$, $B\left (2t_{1}^{2},4t_{1}\right )$, and $C\left (2t_{2}^{2},4t_{2}\right )$ is given as $\left (\frac{7}{3},\frac{4}{3}\right )$.

For the $y$-coordinate :

$\frac{4t_{1}+4t_{2}+0}{3}=\frac{4}{3}⟹4(t_{1}+t_{2})=4⟹t_{1}+t_{2}=1$

For the $x$-coordinate :

$\frac{2t_{1}^{2}+2t_{2}^{2}+2}{3}=\frac{7}{3}⟹2\left (t_{1}^{2}+t_{2}^{2}\right )=5⟹t_{1}^{2}+t_{2}^{2}=\frac{5}{2}$

Find the Relationship between $t_{1}$ and $t_{2}$ : 

Using the identity $(t_{1}+t_{2})^{2}=t_{1}^{2}+t_{2}^{2}+2t_{1}t_{2}$ :

$(1)^{2}=\frac{5}{2}+2t_{1}t_{2}⟹1-\frac{5}{2}=2t_{1}t_{2}⟹2t_{1}t_{2}=-\frac{3}{2}⟹t_{1}t_{2}=-\frac{3}{4}$

Now, calculate $(t_{1}-t_{2})^{2}$ :

$(t_{1}-t_{2})^{2}=(t_{1}+t_{2})^{2}-4t_{1}t_{2}=1^{2}-4\left (-\frac{3}{4}\right )=1+3=4$

Calculate $(BC)^{2}$ The distance formula for $(BC)^{2}$ is :

$(BC)^{2}=(x_{2}-x_{1})^{2}+(y_{2}-y_{1})^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $(BC)^{2}=\left [2\left (t_{2}^{2}-t_{1}^{2}\right )\right ]^{2}+[4(t_{2}-t_{1})]^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $(BC)^{2}=4(t_{2}-t_{1})^{2}(t_{2}+t_{1})^{2}+16(t_{2}-t_{1})^{2}$

Substitute the values $(t_{1}-t_{2})^{2}=4$ and $(t_{1}+t_{2})=1$ :

$(BC)^{2}=4(4)(1)^{2}+16(4)=16+64=80$

solution.body:
The function is defined as :

$f(x)=\lim _{θ\to 0}\left (\frac{\cos πx-x^{\left (\dfrac{2}{θ}\right )}\sin (x-1)}{1+x^{\left (\dfrac{2}{θ}\right )}(x-1)}\right )$

Let $n=\frac{2}{θ}$. As $θ\to 0,n\to \infty$ (specifically, let's consider $θ$ approaching 0 such that the power grows). The behavior of the function depends on the value of $x$ because of the term $x^{n}$.

Case 1 : $|x|<1$ As $n\to \infty ,x^{n}\to 0$.

$f(x)=\frac{\cos πx-0}{1+0}=\cos πx$

Case 2 : $|x|>1$ As $n\to \infty ,x^{n}\to \infty$. We divide the numerator and denominator by $x^{n}$ :

$f(x)=\lim _{n\to \infty }\frac{\frac{\cos πx}{xn}-\sin (x-1)}{\frac{1}{xn}+(x-1)}=\frac{0-\sin (x-1)}{0+(x-1)}=\frac{-\sin (x-1)}{x-1}$

Case 3 : $x=1$ If $x=1$, then $\cos (π)=-1$ and $\sin (0)=0$.

$f(1)=\frac{-1-(1^{n}\cdot 0)}{1+(1^{n}\cdot 0)}=-1$

Case 4 : $x=-1$ If $x=-1$, then $\cos (-π)=-1$ and $\sin (-2)=-\sin (2)$. Since $n=2/θ$ is even, $(-1)^{n}=1$.

$f(-1)=\frac{-1-(1\cdot \sin (-2))}{1+(1\cdot -2)}=\frac{-1+\sin 2}{-1}=1-\sin 2$

So $\mathrm{f}(\mathrm{x})$ become

$f(x)=\left \{\begin{array}{ll} \frac{-\sin (x-1)}{x-1} & \text{if}x\in (-\infty ,-1)\cup (1,\infty ) \\ \cos πx & \text{if}x\in (-1,1) \\ -1 & \text{if}x=1 \\ 1-\sin 2 & \text{if}x=-1 \end{array} \right.$

Analyze the Statements

Statement (I) : $f(x)$ is discontinuous at $x=1$.

Value at $x=1$ : $f(1)=-1$.

Left-hand limit ( $x\to 1^{-}$) : Uses the $|x|<1$ definition: $\lim _{x\to 1^{-}}\cos πx=\cos π=-1$.

Right-hand limit $(x\to 1^{+})$ : Uses the $|x|>1$ definition: $\lim _{x\to 1^{+}}\frac{-\sin (x-1)}{x-1}$. Using the standard limit $\lim _{u\to 0}\frac{\sin u}{u}=1$, this equals -1. Since $LHL=RHL=f(1)$, the function is continuous at $x=1$. 

Conclusion : Statement (I) is False.

Statement (II) : $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=-1$.

Value at $x=-1$ : $f(-1)=1-\sin 2$.

Left-hand limit $(x\to -1^{-})$: Uses $|x|>1$ definition : $\frac{-\sin (-1-1)}{-1-1}=\frac{-\sin (-2)}{-2}=\frac{\sin 2}{-2}$.

Right-hand limit ( $x\to -1^{+}$): Uses $|x|<1$ definition : $\cos (-π)=-1$. 

Since the limits do not match, the function is discontinuous at $x=-1$. 

Conclusion : Statement (II) is False.

Let $S=\frac{6}{3^{26}}+\frac{10\cdot 1}{3^{25}}+\frac{10\cdot 2}{3^{24}}+\frac{10\cdot 2^{2}}{3^{23}}+\cdots +\frac{10\cdot 2^{24}}{3}$

Notice that from the second term onwards, the terms follow a pattern. Let $S^{'}$ be the sum of these terms:

$S^{'}=\frac{10\cdot 2^{0}}{3^{25}}+\frac{10\cdot 2^{1}}{3^{24}}+\frac{10\cdot 2^{2}}{3^{23}}+\cdots +\frac{10\cdot 2^{24}}{3^{1}}$

We can factor out $\frac{10}{3^{25}}$ :

$\begin{array}{l} S^{'}=\dfrac{10}{3^{25}}\left (1+\dfrac{2^{1}}{3^{-1}}+\dfrac{2^{2}}{3^{-2}}+\cdots +\dfrac{2^{24}}{3^{-24}}\right ) \\ S^{'}=\dfrac{10}{3^{25}}\left (2^{0}\cdot 3^{0}+2^{1}\cdot 3^{1}+2^{2}\cdot 3^{2}+\cdots +2^{24}\cdot 3^{24}\right ) \end{array}$

$S^{'}=\frac{10}{3^{25}}\sum\limits _{k=0}^{24}(2\cdot 3)^{k}=\frac{10}{3^{25}}\sum\limits _{k=0}^{24}6^{k}$

Calculate the sum of the GP

The series $\sum\limits _{k=0}^{24}6^{k}$ is a geometric progression with first term $a=1$, common ratio $r=6$, and $n=25$ terms. 

The sum formula is $S_{n}=a\frac{r^{n}-1}{r-1}$ :

$\sum\limits _{k=0}^{24}6^{k}=\frac{6^{25}-1}{6-1}=\frac{6^{25}-1}{5}$

Substituting this back into $S^{'}$ :

$S^{'}=\frac{10}{3^{25}}\left (\frac{6^{25}-1}{5}\right )=\frac{2}{3^{25}}\left (6^{25}-1\right )=\frac{2\cdot 6^{25}}{3^{25}}-\frac{2}{3^{25}}$

Since $6^{25}=(2\cdot 3)^{25}=2^{25}\cdot 3^{25}$ :

$S^{'}=\frac{2\cdot 2^{25}\cdot 3^{25}}{3^{25}}-\frac{2}{3^{25}}=2\cdot 2^{25}-\frac{2}{3^{25}}=2^{26}-\frac{2}{3^{25}}$

Find the total sum $S$ :

Now, add the first term $\frac{6}{3^{26}}$ back to $S^{'}$ :

$S=\frac{6}{3^{26}}+2^{26}-\frac{2}{3^{25}}$

[$\text{Note that,}\frac{6}{3^{26}}=\frac{2\cdot 3}{3^{26}}=\frac{2}{3^{25}}$]

$\Rightarrow$ $S=\frac{2}{3^{25}}+2^{26}-\frac{2}{3^{25}}=2^{26}$

solution.body:
For $x\neq \dfrac{nπ}{2}$ none of $\sin x,\cos x,\tan x,\cot x$ is zero, and $f$ has period $2π$, so the four quadrants give every value of $f$.

First quadrant: all four are positive, so $f=1+1+1+1=4$.

Second quadrant: $\sin x>0$, $\cos x<0$, $\tan x<0$, $\cot x<0$, so $f=1-1-1-1=-2$.

Third quadrant: $\sin x<0$, $\cos x<0$, $\tan x>0$, $\cot x>0$, so $f=-1-1+1+1=0$.

Fourth quadrant: $\sin x<0$, $\cos x>0$, $\tan x<0$, $\cot x<0$, so $f=-1+1-1-1=-2$.

The range is $\{4,0,-2\}$ and the sum of its elements is $4+0+(-2)=2$.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

text: The sum of the coefficients of $x^{499}$ and $x^{500}$ in $(1+x)^{1000}+x(1+x)^{999}+x^{2}(1+x)^{998}+\ldots +x^{1000}$ is :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 28th January Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Let

$S=(1+x)^{1000}+x(1+x)^{999}+x^{2}(1+x)^{998}+\cdots +x^{1000}$

Notice that this is a Geometric Progression (GP) with:

First term (a): $(1+x)^{1000}$

Common ratio $(r):\frac{x}{1+x}$

Number of terms ( $n$ ): 1001

The sum of a GP is given by $S=a\frac{(1-r^{n})}{(1-r)}$. Substituting our values:

$S=(1+x)^{1000}\left [\frac{1-\left (\frac{x}{1+x}\right )^{1001}}{1-\frac{x}{1+x}}\right ]$

Simplify the denominator: $1-\frac{x}{1+x}=\frac{1+x-x}{1+x}=\frac{1}{1+x}$.

$S=(1+x)^{1000}\cdot (1+x)\left [1-\frac{x^{1001}}{(1+x)^{1001}}\right ]$

$S=(1+x)^{1001}-x^{1001}$

Now we need the coefficients of $x^{499}$ and $x^{500}$ in the simplified expression $(1+x)^{1001}-x^{1001}$. 

Since $x^{1001}$ only affects the term with power 1001, we only look at $(1+x)^{1001}$.

In the binomial expansion $(1+x)^{n}$

Coefficient of $x^{r}$ is ${}^{n}C_{r}$

Coefficient of $x^{499}$ in $S$ :

${}^{1001}C_{499}$

Coefficient of $x^{500}$ in $S$ :

${}^{1001}C_{500}$ (The term $x^{1001}$ does not contribute.)

$\text{Sum of coefficients}$

$\begin{array}{l} {}^{1001}C_{499}+{}^{1001}C_{500}={}^{1002}C_{500} \end{array}$

[$\text{Using pascal’s identity}$

${}^{n}C_{r}+{}^{n}C_{r+1}={}^{n+1}C_{r+1}$]

text: If $\sum\limits _{r=1}^{25}\left (\frac{r}{r^{4}+r^{2}+1}\right )=\frac{p}{q}$, where p and q are positive integers such that $\gcd (p,q)=1$, then p + q is equal to $________$.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 28th January Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Given

$\sum\limits _{r=1}^{25}\left (\frac{r}{r^{4}+r^{2}+1}\right )=\frac{p}{q}$

The expression $r^{4}+r^{2}+1$ can be factored using a completion of squares technique:

$r^{4}+r^{2}+1=\left (r^{4}+2r^{2}+1\right )-r^{2}=\left (r^{2}+1\right )^{2}-r^{2}$

Using the difference of squares formula, $a^{2}-b^{2}=(a-b)(a+b)$ :

$r^{4}+r^{2}+1=\left (r^{2}-r+1\right )\left (r^{2}+r+1\right )$

Split into Partial Fractions

Now, let's rewrite the general term $T_{r}$ :

$T_{r}=\frac{r}{(r^{2}-r+1)(r^{2}+r+1)}$

We can express the numerator $r$ in terms of the factors in the denominator:

$\left (r^{2}+r+1\right )-\left (r^{2}-r+1\right )=2r$

So, $r=\frac{1}{2}\left [\left (r^{2}+r+1\right )-\left (r^{2}-r+1\right )\right ]$. Substituting this back:

$T_{r}=\frac{1}{2}\left [\frac{\left (r^{2}+r+1\right )-\left (r^{2}-r+1\right )}{(r^{2}-r+1)(r^{2}+r+1)}\right ]$

$T_{r}=\frac{1}{2}\left [\frac{1}{r^{2}-r+1}-\frac{1}{r^{2}+r+1}\right ]$

Evaluate the Telescoping Sum

Let $f(r)=\frac{1}{r^{2}-r+1}$. 

Note that $f(r+1)=\frac{1}{(r+1)^{2}-(r+1)+1}=\frac{1}{r^{2}+2r+1-r-1+1}=\frac{1}{r^{2}+r+1}$. 

Our sum becomes : $S=\frac{1}{2}\sum\limits _{r=1}^{25}[f(r)-f(r+1)]$

Expanding this:

For $r=1$ : $f(1)-f(2)$

For $r=2:f(2)-f(3)$

For $r=3:f(3)-f(4)$

…

For $r=24:f(24)-f(25)$

For $r=25:f(25)-f(26)$

Result of summation: $\sum\limits _{r=1}^{25}[f(r)-f(r+1)]=f(1)-f(26)$

So,

$S=\frac{1}{2}[f(1)-f(26)]$

Calculate the Final Value

$f(1)=\frac{1}{1^{2}-1+1}=1$

$\begin{array}{l} f(26)=\dfrac{1}{25^{2}+25+1}=\dfrac{1}{625+25+1}=\dfrac{1}{651} \\ S=\dfrac{1}{2}\left [1-\dfrac{1}{651}\right ]=\dfrac{1}{2}\left (\dfrac{651-1}{651}\right )=\dfrac{650}{2\times 651} \\ S=\dfrac{325}{651} \end{array}$

$325=(5)^{2}\times 13$ and $651=3\times 7\times 31$ they share no common factor $\gcd (325,651)=1$ 

So $p=325$ and $q=651\thereforep+q=325+651=976$

text: Three persons enter in a lift at the ground floor. The lift will go up to $10^{th}$ floor. The number of ways, in which the three persons can exit the lift at three different floors, if the lift does not stop at first, second and third floors, is equal to $________$.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 28th January Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Given:

The lift goes up to the $10^{\text{th}}$ floor.

The lift does not stop at $1^{\text{st}},2^{\text{nd}},3^{\text{rd}}$ floors.

So, the persons can get down only at the remaining floors.

$4,5,6,7,8,9,10\Rightarrow 7\text{floors}$

Now, all three persons must exit at three different floors (no two can get down at the same floor).

Also, the three persons are distinct, so who gets down where matters.

First, choose which 3 floors (out of 7) will be used:

${}^{7}C_{3}=\frac{7\cdot 6\cdot 5}{3\cdot 2\cdot 1}=35$

Next, assign (arrange) the 3 distinct persons to these 3 chosen floors:

Number of arrangements of 3 persons:

$3!=6$

So, total number of ways:

$\text{Total ways}={}^{7}C_{3}\times 3!=35\times 6=210$

text: If the distance of the point $P(43,α,β)$, $β<0$, from the line $⃗{r}=4\hat{i}-\hat{k}+μ(2\hat{i}+3\hat{k}),μ\in \mathrm{ℝ}$ along a line with direction ratios $3,-1,0$ is $13\sqrt{10}$, then $α^{2}+β^{2}$ is equal to $________$
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 28th January Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
[IMG]


Point $P$ : $(43,α,β)$ with the constraint $β<0$.

Target Line ( $L_{1}$ ) : Given by $⃗{r}=4\hat{i}-\hat{k}+μ(2\hat{i}+3\hat{k})$. 

A general point $Q$ on this line is $(4+2μ,0,-1+3μ)$.

Direction of measurement : The distance is measured along a line with direction ratios $(3,-1,0)$.

Find Point $Q$ on the Target Line

Since the distance is measured along the direction $d=(3,-1,0)$, the vector $PQ$ must be parallel to $d$.

$\begin{array}{l} PQ=Q-P=(4+2μ-43,0-α,-1+3μ-β) \\ PQ=(2μ-39,-α,3μ-β-1) \\ PQ=(2μ-39,-α,3μ-β-1) \end{array}$

Because $PQ$ is parallel to $(3,-1,0)$, their components must be proportional :

1.$\frac{2μ-39}{3}=\frac{-α}{-1}⟹2μ-39=3α⟹2μ=3α+39$

2.$\frac{3μ-β-1}{0}$ suggests the numerator must be zero for a finite ratio to exist: $3μ-β-1=0⟹β=3μ-1$

Calculate the Distance $PQ$

The distance $PQ$ is given as $13\sqrt{10}$. Using the distance formula on the proportional components where the ratio is $k$ :

$\begin{array}{l} PQ=k(3,-1,0)=(3k,-k,0) \\ |PQ|=\sqrt{(3k)^{2}+(-k)^{2}+0^{2}}=\sqrt{10k^{2}}=|k|\sqrt{10} \end{array}$

Given $|PQ|=13\sqrt{10}$, we find $|k|=13$, so $k=\pm 13$.

Solve for $α,μ$, and $β$

From our proportionality equations :

$-α=-k⟹α=k$

$2μ-39=3k$

Case 1 : $k=13$

$α=13$

$2μ-39=3(13)=39⟹2μ=78⟹μ=39$

$β=3μ-1=3(39)-1=116$

Constraint Check : $β<0$ is False. (Reject this case)

Case 2 : $k=-13$

$α=-13$

$2μ-39=3(-13)=-39⟹2μ=0⟹μ=0$

$β=3(0)-1=-1$

Constraint Check : $β<0$ is True. (Accept this case)

$α^{2}+β^{2}=(-13)^{2}+(-1)^{2}=169+1=170$

The value of $α^{2}+β^{2}$ is 170 .

text: Let $A=\left [\begin{array}{ll} 3 & -4 \\ 1 & -1 \end{array}\right ]$ and $B$ be two matrices such that $A^{100}=100B+I$. Then the sum of all the elements of $B^{100}$ is $_______$
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 28th January Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Decompose Matrix A We can write matrix $A$ as the sum of the Identity matrix $I$ and a $\text{residual matrix}C:$

$\begin{array}{lllllllll} A=I+C=\left [\begin{array}{ll} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{array}\right ]+\left [\begin{array}{ll} 2 & -4 \\ 1 & -2 \end{array}\right ],\text{Let}C=\left [\begin{array}{ll} 2 & -4 \\ 1 & -2 \end{array}\right ]. \\ C^{2}=\left [\begin{array}{ll} 2 & -4 \\ 1 & -2 \end{array}\right ]\left [\begin{array}{ll} 2 & -4 \\ 1 & -2 \end{array}\right ]=\left [\begin{array}{ll} 4-4 & -8+8 \\ 2-2 & -4+4 \end{array}\right ]=\left [\begin{array}{ll} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{array}\right ]=0 \end{array}$

Since $C^{2}=0,C$ is a nilpotent matrix. Consequently, $C^{n}=0$ for all $n\geq 2$.

Find $A^{100}$ using Binomial Expansion :

$A^{100}=(I+C)^{100}={}^{100}C_{0}I^{100}+{}^{100}C_{1}I^{99}C+{}^{100}C_{2}I^{98}C^{2}+\cdots +{}^{100}C_{100}C^{100}$

Since $C^{2}=C^{3}=\cdots =C^{100}=0$, the expansion simplifies to :

$\begin{array}{l} A^{100}={}^{100}C_{0}I+{}^{100}C_{1}C \\ A^{100}=1\cdot I+100\cdot C \\ A^{100}=I+100C \end{array}$

Find Matrix B :

The problem states that $A^{100}=100B+I$. Comparing this to our result:

$\begin{array}{l} 100B+I=100C+I \\ 100B=100C \\ B=C \end{array}$

Calculate the Sum of Elements of $B^{100}$ :

Since $B=C$ and we know $C^{2}=0$, then: $B^{2}=0$

Consequently, $B^{100}=0$ (the zero matrix).

$B^{100}=\left [\begin{array}{ll} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{array}\right ]$ 

The sum of all the elements of $B^{100}$ is 0 .

text:
Let $f$ be a differentiable function satisfying $f(x)=1-2x+\int\limits _{0}^{x}e^{(x-t)}f(t)dt$, $x\in \mathrm{ℝ}$ and let
 $g(x)=\int\limits _{0}^{x}(f(t)+2)^{15}(t-4)^{6}(t+12)^{17}dt$, $x\in \mathrm{ℝ}$.
 If $p$ and $q$ are respectively the points of local minima and local maxima of $g$, then the value of $|p+q|$ is equal to $________$.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 28th January Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The given equation is:

$f(x)=1-2x+\int\limits _{0}^{x}e^{(x-t)}f(t)dt$

Since $e^{(x-t)}=e^{x}\cdot e^{-t}$, we can move $e^{x}$ outside the integral because it is constant relative to $t$

$f(x)=1-2x+e^{x}\int\limits _{0}^{x}e^{-t}f(t)dt$

Differentiate both sides with respect to $x$ using the Leibniz Rule and the product rule:

$f^{'}(x)=-2+\left [e^{x}\int\limits _{0}^{x}e^{-t}f(t)dt+e^{x}(e^{-x}f(x))\right ]$

Now, we use substitution from our original equation. Notice that $e^{x}\int\limits _{0}^{x}e^{-t}f(t)dt=f(x)-(1-2x)$. Substituting this back into the derivative expression:

$f^{'}(x)=-2+[f(x)-1+2x]+f(x)$

$\Rightarrow$ $f^{'}(x)=2f(x)+2x-3$

Combine the terms to get the linear differential equation in the form of $\frac{df(x)}{dx}+P(x)f(x)=Q(x)$

$\frac{df(x)}{dx}-2f(x)=2x-3$

Solve for $f(x)$

Integrating Factor (IF): $e^{\int -2dx}=e^{-2x}$

General Solution: $f(x)\cdot e^{-2x}=\int (2x-3)e^{-2x}dx$

By integrating the right side (Integration by Parts), we get $f(x)=1-x+Ce^{2x}$.

Using $f(0)=1$ (from the original equation), we find $C=0$.

Result: $f(x)=1-x$.

Find the Extrema of $g(x)$

$g(x)=\int\limits _{0}^{x}(f(t)+2)^{15}(t-4)^{6}(t+12)^{17}dt$

Differentiate both sides with respect to $x$ using the Leibniz Rule

$g^{'}(x)=(f(x)+2)^{15}(x-4)^{6}(x+12)^{17}$

Substitute $f(x)=1-x$ :

$\begin{array}{l} g^{'}(x)=(1-x+2)^{15}(x-4)^{6}(x+12)^{17} \\ g^{'}(x)=(3-x)^{15}(x-4)^{6}(x+12)^{17} \end{array}$

Critical points: $x=3,4,-12$.

Plot on number line to find local maxima and minima.


[IMG]

Local Minima ( $p$ ): At $x=-12,g^{'}(x)$ changes sign from negative to positive. Thus, $p=-12$.

Local Maxima ( $q$ ): At $x=3,g^{'}(x)$ changes sign from positive to negative. Thus, $q=3$. 

$x=4$ : No sign change occurs (even power 6), so it is not a local extremum.

Final Answer

$|p+q|=|-12+3|=|-9|=9$

The value of $|p+q|$ is 9 .
